title: PM-2025-02-11: Bursty tail latency + timeouts caused by KV cache fragmentation under burst routing
author: Rafael Mendes
body:
## Summary
On **2025-02-11**, Redwood Hosted API experienced a burst-driven degradation in **p95/p99 latency** and an increase in **request timeouts** in **us-east-1** (primary) with minor spillover impact to **eu-west-1** due to automated overflow routing. The incident was triggered by a combination of:

1) **KV cache fragmentation** in the serving runtime under mixed sequence-length workloads (long-context + short chat) and high churn (many concurrent decode streams completing/evicting).
2) **Burst routing** that concentrated traffic onto a subset of GPU pools during a capacity rebalance, amplifying allocator pressure and making tail latency spikes visible at the fleet level.

Immediate mitigations (traffic shaping, temporary routing overrides, and conservative cache/admission settings) reduced timeouts within ~40 minutes and restored p99 to within SLO guardrails within ~90 minutes. The deeper follow-up work (allocator instrumentation, health dashboards, and a compaction/eviction strategy) became the seed project for **KV cache compaction improvements**.

**Severity:** SEV-1 (customer-facing, multi-tenant hosted impact)

---

## Customer impact
### Affected products
- **Hosted API** (chat/completions and text generation), primarily **us-east-1**.
- Minor secondary impact to **eu-west-1** due to overflow routing during mitigation.

### Impact window
- **Start:** 2025-02-11 18:06 UTC
- **End (timeouts back to baseline):** 2025-02-11 18:47 UTC
- **End (p99 stabilized):** 2025-02-11 19:36 UTC

### What customers saw
- Elevated latency (especially streaming first-token latency and end-to-end decode time).
- Increased 504/499s (client disconnects) and a measurable increase in server-side timeouts.
- Increased rate-limit / overload-style errors in some tenants as admission control became more conservative.

### Quantitative signals (high level)
- **Hosted p99 latency** for the primary chat route in us-east-1 peaked at **~2.6–3.1x** baseline for ~30–45 minutes.
- **Timeout rate** peaked at **~0.8–1.2%** on the affected route (baseline <0.1%).
- **Allocator pressure**: increased KV allocation failures/retries and elevated eviction rate; GPU memory utilization was high but not uniformly saturated, consistent with fragmentation (free memory in unusable holes).

### Customer escalation
- Support ticket(s) were opened during and after the window. Primary thread for hosted timeouts: **SUP-4410**.
- Dedicated customers were not directly impacted by Hosted routing changes, but this incident drove follow-up questions from Dedicated prospects around tail stability (captured in later CS conversations).

---

## Detection
### How we detected
- Automated alert: **Hosted runtime tail-latency SLO burn** (p99) in us-east-1.
- Secondary alerts:
  - Elevated timeout/error rate on chat route
  - Increased GPU pool eviction rate (existing signal)

### Detection gap
We did **not** have a first-class, oncall-friendly fragmentation signal at the time. We inferred fragmentation indirectly from:
- Rising allocation retries/failures
- Spiky eviction behavior
- GPU memory usage that appeared “high but not maxed” while allocator was failing

This postmortem includes follow-ups to add explicit fragmentation metrics and dashboard panels.

---

## Timeline (UTC)
> Times below reflect the primary us-east-1 hosted pool. Some actions were performed in parallel by Runtime and SRE.

- **18:06** – Alert fires: p99 latency burn for hosted chat route in us-east-1.
- **18:08** – Oncall (SRE) acknowledges; begins triage. Initial suspicion: capacity imbalance + burst.
- **18:11** – Error rate increases; multiple tenants show timeouts. Incident declared **SEV-1**; incident channel created.
- **18:14** – Quick checks: no ongoing deploy, no control plane errors; GPU pool utilization high; scheduler queue depth spiky.
- **18:17** – Runtime oncall pulled in; notes increased KV eviction rate and allocator churn in logs.
- **18:21** – Mitigation #1: apply temporary routing override to spread traffic across additional pools/regions (reduce concentration).
- **18:26** – Mitigation #2: adjust admission control / concurrency limits for the most impacted pool to stabilize (trade throughput for tail).
- **18:31** – Timeouts begin dropping; p99 still elevated with periodic spikes.
- **18:34** – Hypothesis confirmed: KV cache fragmentation under bursty churn; allocator searching/relocating causes stalls; occasional allocation failure path is expensive.
- **18:38** – Mitigation #3: reduce effective KV cache target size per request class (tighten limits for long-context) to reduce worst-case fragmentation and OOM risk.
- **18:47** – Timeouts return near baseline; incident remains open to monitor tail.
- **19:02** – Tail latency continues improving; spillover routing reverted gradually.
- **19:36** – p99 stabilizes within normal guardrails; incident resolved.
- **20:10** – Draft customer-facing summary provided to Support for active tickets.
- **2025-02-12** – Internal review: confirm need for allocator instrumentation and compaction strategy; project proposal drafted.

---

## Root cause
**Primary root cause:** The serving runtime’s KV cache allocator exhibited **high fragmentation** under bursty, mixed sequence-length traffic with high decode churn. Fragmentation created many “holes” in the KV cache memory space, increasing allocator overhead and elevating the probability of expensive allocation/eviction paths.

Under fragmentation, the runtime spent additional time:
- Searching for contiguous or suitably-sized blocks
- Evicting and re-allocating blocks more frequently
- Hitting slow-path failure handling when a request could not be satisfied with available contiguous capacity

This manifested as **bursty p95/p99 spikes** and increased timeouts when combined with routing concentration.

---

## Contributing factors
1) **Burst routing concentration during capacity rebalance**
   - A portion of traffic was steered into a smaller set of GPU pools, increasing churn and pushing the allocator into pathological regimes.

2) **Mixed workload distribution (long-context + short requests)**
   - Variable context lengths increased block utilization variance and left unusable holes when sequences completed.

3) **Insufficient allocator/fragmentation observability**
   - We lacked direct, actionable metrics for fragmentation ratio, compaction cost (none existed), and allocation slow-path attribution.

4) **Eviction policy not scheduler-aware**
   - Victim selection did not sufficiently incorporate scheduler priorities/tiers, causing local unfairness and amplifying tail for some tenants.

5) **Slow-path cost surfaced as latency (not just throughput)**
   - Slow allocation/eviction happened on the critical path for some requests, directly impacting tail latency.

---

## Immediate mitigations applied
### Mitigations that helped
- **Traffic spreading / routing overrides** to reduce concentration and smooth burst impacts.
- **Tighter admission control** for impacted pools to reduce allocator churn and stabilize p99.
- **Temporary long-context constraints** to reduce worst-case KV pressure and OOM risk.

### Mitigations with known tradeoffs
- Admission control changes reduced throughput and increased queuing for some tenants.
- Long-context constraints increased the rate of early rejections for a subset of requests.

### What we explicitly avoided
- Any runtime changes requiring binary rollout during the incident.
- Aggressive restarts of GPU pools (risked further load concentration and cold-cache effects).

---

## What went well
- Oncall response was fast; SEV-1 declared early, and runtime/SRE coordination was effective.
- Routing overrides reduced timeouts quickly.
- No data integrity issues; impact was isolated to latency/availability.

## What went poorly
- Lack of fragmentation-first observability prolonged diagnosis; we relied on indirect signals.
- Existing dashboards were not sufficient to attribute tail latency spikes to allocator slow-paths.
- Mitigation runbook guidance for fragmentation-specific incidents was incomplete at the time.

---

---

## Customer communications
- Support provided impacted customers a brief summary: “bursty traffic causing elevated tail latency; mitigations applied; no data issues.”
- Product alignment: We explicitly avoided promising a specific model change; messaging focused on “runtime memory management improvements” and “latency stability work” with staged rollout.
- For enterprise conversations, we used this incident to justify the roadmap item: compaction/eviction strategy + stronger observability, with a canary-first rollout plan.

---

## Lessons learned
1) **Tail latency stability is as much a memory-management problem as a scheduling problem** in modern LLM serving.
2) **Fragmentation needs a direct metric** (not inferred) to shorten MTTR.
3) Burst routing and pool rebalancing must consider **allocator health** as a first-class constraint (not only utilization/queue depth).
4) Any compaction solution must be **budgeted and scheduler-aware** to avoid trading p99 spikes for median regressions.

---

## Appendix
### A. Triage signals we used (during incident)
- Route-level p95/p99 latency, timeout rate
- GPU pool utilization + queue depth
- Existing eviction counters (coarse)
- Runtime logs indicating allocator retries/failures

### B. Signals we are adding (post-incident)
- Fragmentation ratio (definition to be standardized in runtime architecture page)
- Allocation slow-path counters + latency attribution
- Eviction rate labeled by reason (pressure vs policy)
- Compaction cost metrics (bytes moved, GPU time, sync wait)

### C. References
- Known issue entry: KV cache fragmentation under bursts
- Runbook: mitigating fragmentation incidents
- KV cache compaction improvements: design doc + ADRs
- Linear umbrella: ENG-2841
